summary: Defines how a SIP user agent can tell other user agents and its registrar what it can do, by adding feature parameters to the Contact header field. This allows requests to be routed to devices that can handle them, such as ones that support video.

eli5.summary: Your phone can tell callers, "I can do voice, video and text." so they pick the right way to reach you. This document says how it writes that on its name tag.

questions: how do sip contact header feature parameters work
subtitle: How a SIP device can describe what it can do by adding feature parameters to its Contact header.

tldr.problem: SIP user agents vary widely, from videophones to voice-only phones to servers, but SIP had no general way for one element to learn what a user agent can do or what kind of device it is.
tldr.mechanism: A user agent describes itself as a feature set built from media feature tags and encodes it as parameters of the Contact header field, in REGISTER requests, OPTIONS responses and dialog-creating messages.
tldr.outcome: Registrars and other elements can use this information, for example to route a request to a device that supports video. The RFC also registers 18 initial SIP feature tags and warns that the information is sensitive.

today: RFC 3840 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is paired with RFC 3841, which covers caller preferences.

sections.title: Why User Agents Describe Themselves
sections.content:
SIP user agents (UAs) differ a lot in capabilities and in the devices they represent. The RFC gives three motivating cases. A PC application wants to grey out interface features that a limited peer device does not support. A caller wants video, so the call should be routed to the user's videophone rather than the voice-only wireless phone. A network application wants to know whether a UA can receive a MESSAGE request before sending one, which needs capabilities to be stored at registration.

SIP already has the Allow, Accept, Accept-Language and Supported header fields, but they convey only a small part of what is needed. They describe the UA only as it applies to one request, and SIP cannot convey characteristics, meaning information that describes the UA itself.

RFC 3840 therefore carries capability and characteristic information as parameters of the Contact header field, usable in REGISTER requests and responses, OPTIONS responses, and requests and responses that create dialogs such as INVITE.
sections.eli5: A phone needs a way to tell others what it is good at. Otherwise a video call might get sent to a phone with no screen.

sections.title: Feature Tags and the Content Negotiation Framework
sections.content:
The design reuses terms from the IETF content negotiation work (RFC 2506, RFC 2533, RFC 2738 and RFC 2703). A feature tag is a name that identifies a feature, such as sip.methods. A feature set describes everything an entity can handle, and a feature collection is one specific point in that space.

For a SIP UA, a feature collection is an instantaneous modality: a snapshot of what the UA is doing at that moment. This decides how to model things. Properties that a UA can exhibit at the same time, such as audio and video, must be separate feature tags. SIP methods can be values of one tag (sip.methods) because a UA processes a single request at a time. The RFC admits the model has weaknesses but calls it a useful guideline.

The RFC also separates a capability, which may or may not be used in a call, from a characteristic, a non-negotiable property such as being a mobile phone. The semantics do not distinguish them, and the word capability covers both.
sections.eli5: Each skill gets its own label. Things you can do at the same moment, like talking and showing video, need separate labels.

sections.title: Encoding a Feature Set in Contact Parameters
sections.content:
A UA builds a contact predicate: an AND (conjunction) of terms, where each term covers one feature tag and may be an OR (disjunction) of simple filters over that tag's values. Each term becomes one feature parameter in the Contact header field. A UA SHOULD give complete information, and when it registers a tag it MUST list all the values it supports.

Naming follows fixed rules. For the base tags defined in this document, the leading sip. is stripped, so they appear without a prefix. Any other tag keeps its sip. if it has one and gets a leading +. A boolean TRUE has no value. A disjunction becomes a quoted, comma-separated list. A negation starts with !. Numeric values start with a hash sign, and string values are wrapped in angle brackets. There MUST be only one instance of any feature tag in the parameters.

The UA MUST NOT list methods, event packages, schemes or option tags that are not standardized in IETF standards track RFCs when using sip.methods, sip.events, sip.schemes or sip.extensions. Registered tags in the SIP, IETF or global trees may be used.
sections.eli5: The phone turns its list of skills into a short line of code on its name tag, always the same way, so anyone can read it.

sections.title: Registrations
sections.content:
When a UA registers a contact that represents a UA instance, the common case, it SHOULD include a feature set. If the contact is an address-of-record or something that one feature set cannot describe, it SHOULD NOT. A feature parameter can only be attached to an address-of-record if all devices bound to it share the same values for that parameter.

A REGISTER request MAY carry a Require header field with the value pref if the client wants to be sure the registrar understands these extensions. Without it, a registrar that does not understand the extension simply ignores the Contact parameters. When a UA refreshes its registration it MUST repeat its feature parameters if it wants them to stay active, and a registrar's 200 OK MUST include all feature parameters associated with each Contact URI.

If a UA registers against several addresses-of-record with different capabilities, it MUST use different URIs in each registration. The Allow, Accept, Accept-Language and Allow-Events header fields in a REGISTER serve a different purpose and are not a substitute for the feature parameters.
sections.eli5: When the phone signs in, it hands over its name tag. If it signs in again later, it has to show the tag again or the office forgets it.

sections.title: Dialogs and OPTIONS
sections.content:
Outside registration, a UAC or UAS MAY add feature parameters to the Contact header field of target refresh requests and responses, and they MAY change mid-dialog to signal a change in capabilities. A UAS that receives an OPTIONS request MAY add them to its OPTIONS response, and SHOULD reuse the parameters it registered.

Some feature tags overlap with existing header fields: Allow and sip.methods, Accept and type, Accept-Language and language, and Allow-Events and sip.events. When a header field exists for a capability, a UA MUST use the header field, and a receiver that sees both MUST use the header field and not the feature tag.
sections.eli5: The phone can show its name tag during a call or when asked. If there is already an official form for the same fact, the form wins over the tag.

sections.title: The Base Feature Tags
sections.content:
Section 10 defines the initial tags, all registered in the new SIP tree with the sip. prefix. Boolean media tags are sip.audio, sip.video, sip.text, sip.application, sip.data and sip.control. These indicate media types usable in streams, matching SDP, and not the MIME types the UA can receive (that is the type tag).

Other tags describe the device: sip.automata (voicemail server, conference server, IVR or recording device rather than a human), sip.class (business or personal), sip.duplex (full, half, receive-only, send-only), sip.mobility (fixed or mobile, and cordless phones count as fixed), and sip.description (free text such as make and model).

The rest describe support: sip.events (event packages), sip.methods (methods the UA can receive), sip.extensions (option tags it would put in a Supported header), sip.schemes (URI schemes it can send requests to), sip.priority, sip.actor (principal, attendant, msg-taker or information) and sip.isfocus (the UA is a conference server).
sections.eli5: The tags are like stickers: 'has video', 'is a robot, not a person', 'stays at home', 'takes messages'. Callers can look at the stickers to choose.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The tags reveal sensitive information. Capability data such as media types, methods and extensions might be used for industrial espionage. Mobility, priority and isfocus reveal how a device is used, and tags such as language reveal information about the user. Applications SHOULD provide confidentiality. Because routing decisions, for example under caller preferences, can depend on the values, an attacker who changes them could affect behavior, so integrity SHOULD be provided and authenticity guaranteed.

For registrations, the RFC says to address them to a SIPS URI and have the registrar challenge the UA with digest over TLS. For OPTIONS responses and dialog-initiating messages, the UA SHOULD check with the user before revealing capabilities, and SHOULD warn the user if the requester's identity cannot be verified. S/MIME MAY be used.
sections.eli5: A name tag that says a lot about you should only be shown to people you trust, and nobody should be able to scribble on it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC creates the SIP Media Feature Tag Registration Tree with the prefix sip.. New entries need IETF consensus, which requires publishing an RFC, using the template from RFC 2506. Registrations use the unencoded name, so the registry holds sip.gruu and not +sip.gruu.

It registers the base feature tags, each with an ASN.1 identifier (for example 1.3.6.1.8.4.1 for sip.audio), and one SIP option tag, pref, used in a Require header field of a registration to ensure the registrar supports the caller preferences extensions.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps an official list of the labels, so everyone uses the same words.
